Hi -

I am having difficulty adding telemetry data and I'm hoping someone can help. I have formatted my data following the description in the secr telemetry vignette. The first few rows of my data are:

BM16_17 F2 20 671887 6339907
BM16_17 F2 20 671892.2 6339907
BM16_17 F2 20 671723.2 6340445
BM16_17 F2 21 670293.7 6342067
BM16_17 F2 21 669099.8 6342688
BM16_17 F2 21 669099.1 6342686

When I attempt to load the telemetry data:
CHt <- read.telemetry(file = "telemetry_UTM.txt")

I get the warning message "Telemetry data (telemetryxy) do not match capture histories." I cannot figure out how to resolve this.

I have matched the occasion number to the occasion number in my trapping file. For example, a date of November 30th corresponds to occasion 20 in the trapping file so I called a telemetry location from November 30th occasion 20 as well. Perhaps that is not correct?

If I ignore the warning and go on to combine the trapping and telemetry data:
combinedCH <- addTelemetry (CHBM, CHt, type = c("dependent"), collapsetelemetry = TRUE, verify = TRUE)

I get another warning message:
In addTelemetry(CHBM, CHt, type = c("dependent"), collapsetelemetry = TRUE,  : covariates in telemetryCH do not match detectionCH so covariates discarded

The covariates in my detection CH include 'sex' and 'trap type' but there are no covariates in the telemetryCH. Again, I'm not sure how to resolve this error.

I've plotted the data and the plots seem ok.

If I continue to ignore the warning messages and attempt to run a model:
m0.combined <- secr.fit(combinedCH, model=list(D~1,g0~1,sigma~1), mask = maskBM, detectfn = 'HHN', trace = FALSE)

messages.subject_clean: Sampling design for a clustered population
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe
I'm cautious on this because I suspect/believe that increasing sampling intensity in high density areas causes bias unless handled carefully (I opened a file on this a few years ago but haven't progressed it). However, stratification does make sense. From my amateur understanding of classical stratification, poor definition of strata just reduces the benefit (variance reduction) rather than causing bias. Nor do I see a risk of bias in estimating a density gradient with arbitrarily placed samples - again it's a matter of efficiency.
Murray

On Tuesday, December 31, 2019 at 3:57:03 AM UTC+13, Joseph Clark wrote:
> We are studying an elk population that tends to be clustered around forest openings.  We are planning to use line transect sampling to collect and genotype elk scats for secr analysis.  Most of the elk fecal samples will be in these openings (fields) so we want to adequately sample those areas.  However, a random or systematic sampling design across elk range would result in us spending a lot of time in areas where there are few if any elk.  We have run some simulations with different sampling intensities in grid cells that we have designated as high density and low density, with greater sampling intensity in the high density cells.  The estimates seem okay with little bias.  However, my question is what if we are wrong in assigning the high density and low density cells?  For example, if high elk densities in reality extend further into the low density cells than we thought, will this present a bias?  So far, our simulations suggest no, but I was looking to see if there was a theoretical reason why this sampling approach might be flawed.
>
> Alternatively, we were interested in estimating elk densities as a linear or quadratic function of the distance from fields.  I know that could be done, but would there be a bias if we adjusted our sampling effort the same way?  I know there are adaptive sampling approaches that might be used but I figured that since we have a pretty good idea that elk densities are going to be positively related to the fields, using that information to develop a sampling regime would be preferred.  Thanks!
> Joe

Hi all,

This is my first attempt at using secr so apologies if my explanation is unclear.

I am using secr to try to estimate density of skink populations and my issue is regarding how to add daily temperature to my models as a session-specific time varying covariate.

I have 16 trapping grids (of 25 traps, at 2m spacing) spread between two cities that have been monitored daily for 7-10 day periods three times over the course of my study (Nov 17, Jan 18 and Nov 18). I'm treating populations as closed within each period and am only using captures of one species.

To analyse, my approach has been to model each trapping period separately including all sites together as 'sessions' using:

Nov17 <- read.capthist("~/secr/Nov17.txt", "~/secr/trapfile.txt",
                         detector = "multi")

Jan18 <- read.capthist("~/secr/Jan18.txt", "~/secr/trapfile.txt",
                         detector = "multi")

                         detector = "multi")

fit_Nov17<-secr.fit(Nov17, start = list(D=1000, g0 = 0.01, sigma = 1), model = D ~session, buffer = 10, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE) ### not sure if all these arguments are required

fit_Nov17<-summary(fit_Nov17)

fit_Nov17<-secr.fit(Nov17, start = list(D=1000, g0 = 0.01, sigma = 1), model = list(D~session, g0~tcov), buffer = 10, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE, timecov = c(21.2, 19.3, 20.0, 21.1, 20.9, 19.4, 20.7))

Is this possible or would it be best to model the trapping periods of each city separately (this would greatly reduce my already small sample size)?

Any advice or assistance would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if more detail is needed to understand the problem.

Many thanks

Chris

messages.subject_clean: How to estimate individual encounter probabilities when sigma estimates for both mixture classes differ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am working on a my master's project using a spatially explicit capture-recapture approach to model the exposure of whale watching boats on sperm whales in the Central Azores.
I am analyzing my capture-recapture data using the R 'secr' package to develop different models accounting for sampling effort and heterogeneity in sigma or/and g0 (a detailed list of the models used and outputs is attached below). The model parameters are used for estimating encounter probabilities for each individual in each 1x1km2 grid cell. My results indicate that the best fitting model for my data is based on a half-normal detection function, accounting for heterogeneity in sigma.
As the output of the secr model fit includes two different estimates for sigma for both mixture classes, I am not sure, which of this estimates to use for calculating the individual encounter probabilities. In comparison, the values for the lambda0 estimates are equal in both mixture classes, so I don't have to choose.
What is the difference between the two estimated parameters? How do I decide which of them to use?
As they yield quite different results in the further probability estimates, it would be important for me to understand how this model estimates the parameters and how to interpret the model output.

I am greatly appreciating any help on this topic!

Chiara

Example of the modeling process

model.used<-secr.fit(secr.obj,model=list(g0~1,sigma~h2),mask=hab.mask,detectfn=0,trace=F)
predict(model.used)
$`session = 1, h2 = 1`
       link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
D       log 1.155845e-03 6.010725e-04 4.430554e-04 3.015373e-03
g0    logit 6.702131e-02 2.025034e-02 3.668150e-02 1.193466e-01
sigma   log 1.227834e+04 2.172605e+03 8.703262e+03 1.732196e+04
pmix  logit 5.357822e-02 4.429945e-02 1.011249e-02 2.387997e-01

$`session = 1, h2 = 2`
       link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
D       log 1.155845e-03 6.010725e-04 4.430554e-04 3.015373e-03
g0    logit 6.702131e-02 2.025034e-02 3.668150e-02 1.193466e-01
sigma   log 2.563491e+03 8.098543e+02 1.400525e+03 4.692157e+03
pmix  logit 9.464218e-01 4.429945e-02 7.612003e-01 9.898875e-01

#Estimating individual encounter probabilities for each 1x1km2 grid cell of the habitat mask

number.animals<-attributes(secr.obj)$dim[1]

pr.int <http://pr.int><-array(0,c(length(hab.mask[,1]),number.animals)) #Creates a matrix of zeros, with the same number of rows as grid cells in the habitat mask (j) and the same number of columns as marked individuals (i)

for(i in 1:number.animals){                                     #A loop for every individual that was marked
  pdf<-fxi.secr(model.used,i=i,X=hab.mask)                        #Estimates the probability density function of the home range centers for individual i for every cell in the habitat mask
  pr<-array(0,c(length(hab.mask[,1]),length(hab.mask[,1])))       #Storage matrix for encounter probabilities. Creates a matrix of zeros, with the same number of rows and columns as the number of cells in the habitat mask
  for(j in 1:length(hab.mask[,1])){                           #Runs a loop for every cell in the habitat mask
    #Estimates the probability of encountering individual i for every grid cell in the habitat mask, when the home range center of individual i is located in grid cell j. The probability is estimated over 1 SO (i.e. 1 second)
    enc.prob<-1-exp(-lamda*exp((-(sqrt(abs(hab.mask$x[j]-hab.mask$x)^2+abs(hab.mask$y[j]-hab.mask$y)^2)^2))/(2*sigma^2))) #Half normal detection function
    pr[,j]<-enc.prob*pdf[j]     #Multiplies the estimated encounter probabilities with the probability density function of cell j in the habitat mask (part of the spatial integration)
  }
  pr.int <http://pr.int>[,i]<-rowSums(pr)         #Adds the sum for each cell in the habitat mask for individual i (integrates the results over all cells in the habitat mask for individual i)
}

I'm looking for some feedback on the effect bk is having in my model. I am using secr 4.1.0 and am working with camera trap data from wolverines. 77 detections of 7 animals.

In all models I used a mask that included a 40 km buffer around trap locations. The suggest.buffer function recommended a 31 km buffer. RPSV(CHBM, CC = TRUE) = 6814.49, so 4 times that recommends ~28 km buffer. Other literature had used 40 km, so I rounded up and went with a 40 km buffer to be safe. Spacing was 2500.

I then used the code:
mask.check(m2, buffers = c(30000, 40000, 50000), spacings = c(1500, 2500, 3500), LL = FALSE, file = "m2.maskcheck")
to evaluate the influence of buffer size on density, and ideally confirm that I had used an appropriate buffer size.

For models with bk it seems that a buffer size of about 80 km is needed before density estimates stabilize. The bk covariate also has a big effect on density and sigma estimates. Hi Andrea,

I'm not 100% sure this explains the behavior you are seeing, but I believe my explanation is consistent with all the evidence you present here. Hopefully others will chime in, too.

Here is an enumerated list of points that I think are relevant.

1. First of all, looking at your plot of spatial recaptures on the trapping array suggests to me that sigma may not be identifiable. This is just an intuition based on my prior experience. The scale of individual movement is pretty close to the size of the trapping array and I've seen identifiability go either way in this case. It turns out, though, that sigma is identifiable with this data set under M0.

2. Here is a result I'm pretty confident in, though I haven't confirmed it or seen it confirmed in the literature. When the extent of individual movement is approaching the extent of the trapping array, under M0, the true value of p0 will play a role in whether or not sigma is identifiable. If you lower the true p0 enough, sigma will no longer be identifiable, because capture events at the tail of the detection function become increasingly rare.

3. When you include a bk effect when there is trap happy behavior, p0.p (first capture p0) goes down considerably. In your case, it goes down an order of magnitude.

4. Under trap happy Mb, the first capture events (all data up to the first capture at each trap) overwhelmingly inform the estimation of sigma when you have many traps with no captures. The majority of individual by trap by occasion data are possible or actual first capture events. All data for traps with no captures are possible first capture events that did not happen. Therefore, the p0.p estimate has a high "leverage" on the sigma estimate.

Combine 2 - 4. The lowering of first capture p0 under M0 (which is just p0 because all events have the same baseline detection probability) to that under Mb (p0.p), an order of magnitude drop, made sigma no longer identifiable.

Do the parameter estimates ever stabilize as you increase the buffer? If not, I think sigma is not identifiable under Mb for this data set, whether my explanation is correct or not.

Ben

Hi -

Murray, I looked into this a bit more. For 2 of the individuals, all of the re-detections occurred at the initial site. Thank you both. I really appreciate your help sorting through this.

Andrea

Hello Chiara
I do not have a straight answer and nor it seems does anyone else. The question is outside normal usage (we don't usually want to collapse the heterogeneous sigma to a single average value) and not specific to SECR, so it might help to consult a friendly statistician. Model averaging is not mysterious - you can do it yourself on one line with the AIC model weights and the standard formulae (SE a little harder, but still do-able). I would compute the weighted sigma for the h2 model, as discussed before, and model average that with sigma from the other model.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I work with multiple threatened species inside an 1100ha fenced reserve. I need to estimate the density of these species. One of my species, the boodie (Bettongia lesueur) is extremely trap-happy whereas the second species, the golden bandicoot, is only moderately trap-happy. Despite our best efforts to make traps more species-specific, the high trappability of boodies is interfering with my ability to estimate the density of bandicoots. Point in case, a sudden decline in the abundance of boodies (normal decline due to desert conditions) saw my density estimate for bandicoots jump 10-fold. I need to deal with heterogeneity in trappability caused by the presence of a second species with dramatic population fluctuations.

Is there anyway I can incorporate capture data for 2 species simultaneously in openCR?

Can I use species as a covariate in the capthist file, include species in the model and expect better estimates of density for each species?

Thanks,

Cheryl
